name: Amitriptyline
summary: Amitriptyline is a prescription-only medicine from a group called tricyclic antidepressants, used for nerve pain and to help prevent migraine, and also for depression. Taking more than the prescribed amount can cause serious effects such as changes in heartbeat and seizures (fits), so the NHS says to call 999 now if symptoms follow and to contact NHS 111 for advice.
usedFor: Nerve pain (neuralgia) and other pain that lasts a long time
Depression, where the doses used are higher than those used for pain
howItWorks: Amitriptyline belongs to a group of medicines called tricyclic antidepressants, which are thought to work by increasing levels of a chemical in the brain called serotonin. For pain, the NHS says it is thought to change how nerves handle pain signals as well as raising serotonin.
onset: Some people start to feel better after 1 or 2 weeks, but it can take 6 weeks for amitriptyline to work as a painkiller.

common: Common side effects include feeling sleepy, dizziness, a dry mouth, constipation and sweating.
Less common side effects include fainting, trembling, an irregular heartbeat, blurred vision or problems passing water.
The NHS says common side effects often go away within a few days as the body adjusts.
For constipation the NHS suggests more fibre such as fruit, vegetables and cereals, plenty of water and regular exercise.
For a dry mouth the NHS suggests chewing sugar-free gum or sucking sugar-free sweets.
For dizziness the NHS suggests drinking plenty of fluids and standing up slowly, and not driving, cycling or using tools or machines while dizzy.
For trouble passing urine the NHS suggests relaxing, not forcing the flow, and trying again a short while later.
serious: A fast or irregular heartbeat, yellowing of the skin or eyes, headache with confusion, weakness or muscle cramps, or eye pain, vision changes, or eye swelling or redness are signs for which the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 now.
Being unable to pass urine at all needs urgent advice from a doctor.
The NHS says to call 999 for signs of a stroke, a seizure (fit) or severe chest pain, and not to drive to A&E.

A serious allergic reaction is rare, but the NHS says to call 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or struggling breathing, a tight throat or difficulty swallowing, or a swollen, itchy or blistered skin rash.
Taking more than the prescribed amount can cause serious effects such as a change in heartbeat and seizures (fits), and the NHS pain page advises contacting NHS 111 for advice.

The NHS depression page says to call 999 now if more than the prescribed dose has been taken and there is a fast or irregular heartbeat, a seizure, drowsiness or passing out, difficulty breathing, or sudden very bad confusion.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E now for thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life.
NHS 111 is open 24 hours every day, and Samaritans is a free line on 116 123.

cautions: The NHS says to tell the doctor before starting about a past allergic reaction to amitriptyline or any other medicine, heart problems, epilepsy, glaucoma, liver or kidney problems, difficulty emptying the bladder or diabetes.
The NHS says it can be dangerous to take amitriptyline with methadone, stimulants such as MDMA or cocaine, hallucinogens such as LSD, and some new psychoactive substances.
Cannabis with amitriptyline can cause strong sleepiness and a fast heartbeat.
Some antidepressants can affect how amitriptyline works, including ones taken in the past.
A Guy's and St Thomas' NHS page says many medicines can interfere with amitriptyline and that the doctor and pharmacist need to know about it before another medicine is started or stopped.
The same page advises against the herbal remedy St John's wort.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk with amitriptyline but may add to sleepiness, and it is usually best to stop drinking until the effect of the medicine is known.
The NHS says amitriptyline can be taken during pregnancy and is not thought to be harmful to the baby.
The NHS says it can be taken while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy, because only very small amounts pass into breast milk.
The NHS advises stopping driving and cycling, and avoiding machinery or tools, for the first few days until the effect of the medicine is known.
Stopping suddenly can cause extra side effects, so the NHS says to talk to the doctor before stopping.
monitoring: The NHS says the doctor usually lowers the dose gradually over several weeks, or longer after long-term use, when treatment stops. One migraine leaflet from an NHS trust says treatment is often reviewed after about 6 to 12 months of good control, and that it is not a cure, so it might need to be restarted if headaches become frequent again.

references.title: NHS: How and when to take amitriptyline for depression

sections.heading: What is amitriptyline used for?
sections.body:
Amitriptyline is a prescription-only medicine. It is used to treat nerve pain, called neuralgia, and other pain that lasts a long time. It is also used to help prevent migraines. It is used to treat depression too, and the doses used to treat pain are lower than the doses used for depression.

It comes as tablets and as a liquid that is swallowed. A pain clinic leaflet says it is usually kept for pain that stays troublesome despite standard painkillers such as paracetamol and codeine. Amitriptyline belongs to a group of medicines called tricyclic antidepressants. The NHS says it does not work any better or worse than other antidepressants when it is used for depression.

sections.heading: How does amitriptyline work, and how long does it take?
sections.body:
Tricyclic antidepressants are thought to work by increasing levels of a chemical in the brain called serotonin. For pain, the NHS says amitriptyline is also thought to change how nerves handle pain signals. Sleep can improve quite soon, but pain relief usually takes 1 or 2 weeks to start. Some people start to feel better after 1 or 2 weeks, but it can take 6 weeks for amitriptyline to work as a painkiller. The NHS advises allowing at least 6 weeks to see whether it works for pain.

For depression, it usually takes between 4 and 6 weeks to feel the full benefit. The NHS says it is best taken in the evening or before bed, because it can make a person sleepy. The NHS page on amitriptyline for depression says a forgotten dose is skipped if the next one is nearly due. It also says two doses are never taken together and an extra dose is never taken to make up for a forgotten one.

sections.heading: What are the side effects?
sections.body:
Common side effects include feeling sleepy, dizziness, a dry mouth, constipation and sweating. Less common side effects include fainting, trembling, an irregular heartbeat, blurred vision or problems passing water. The NHS says common side effects often go away within a few days as the body adjusts. The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using tools or machines while feeling sleepy, tired or dizzy.

Serious side effects are rare. The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 now for a fast or irregular heartbeat, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. It gives the same advice for headache with confusion, weakness or muscle cramps, which can be a sign of low sodium in the blood. The NHS says to call 999 for signs of a stroke, a seizure (fit) or severe chest pain. A serious allergic reaction is rare, and the NHS also says to call 999 for it.

sections.heading: What happens if too much is taken?
sections.body:
A formulary note from an NHS area describes amitriptyline as a sedating tricyclic with a high rate of side effects that can be fatal in overdose. The NHS pain page says taking more than the prescribed dose can cause serious effects such as a change in heartbeat and seizures (fits), and advises contacting NHS 111 for advice. The NHS depression page says to call 999 now if more than the prescribed dose has been taken and there is a fast or irregular heartbeat, a seizure, drowsiness or passing out, difficulty breathing, or sudden very bad confusion.

MedlinePlus says an overdose means taking more than the normal or recommended amount, by accident or on purpose. It says people who swallow too much of this medicine are almost always admitted to hospital, and the faster a person gets medical help, the better the chance of recovery.

The NHS says anyone who has seriously harmed themselves, for example by taking an overdose, or who feels they may be about to, should call 999 or go straight to A&E. NHS 111 is open 24 hours every day, and Samaritans is a free line on 116 123. Thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life while taking amitriptyline are a reason to call 999 or go to A&E now, according to the NHS.

sections.heading: Alcohol, other medicines, pregnancy and who needs extra care
sections.body:
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk with amitriptyline but may add to sleepiness, and it is usually best to stop drinking until the effect of the medicine is known. It can be dangerous to take amitriptyline with methadone, stimulants such as MDMA or cocaine, hallucinogens such as LSD, and some new psychoactive substances. Cannabis with amitriptyline can cause strong sleepiness and a fast heartbeat. A Guy's and St Thomas' NHS page says many medicines can interfere with amitriptyline and advises against St John's wort.

The NHS says to tell the doctor before starting about a past allergic reaction to amitriptyline or any other medicine, heart problems, epilepsy, glaucoma, liver or kidney problems, difficulty emptying the bladder or diabetes. The NHS says amitriptyline can be taken during pregnancy and is not thought to be harmful to the baby. It says it can be taken while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy, because only very small amounts pass into breast milk.

sections.heading: Stopping amitriptyline
sections.body: Stopping suddenly can cause extra side effects, including flu-like symptoms. The NHS says not to stop suddenly without talking to a doctor. The NHS also says not to stop just because the medicine seems not to be helping. The NHS says the doctor usually lowers the dose gradually over several weeks, or longer after long-term use. For depression, the NHS says to continue for several months after feeling better, because stopping too soon can bring the depression back. A migraine leaflet from an NHS trust says treatment is often reviewed after about 6 to 12 months of good control, and that it is not a cure, so it might need to be restarted if headaches become frequent again.

faqs.q: Is amitriptyline an antidepressant if it is prescribed for pain?
faqs.a: Amitriptyline belongs to a group of medicines called tricyclic antidepressants. It is used to treat nerve pain and to help prevent migraines, and also to treat depression. The doses used to treat pain are lower than the doses used for depression. For pain, the NHS says it is thought to change how nerves handle pain signals.

faqs.q: How long does amitriptyline take to work for pain?
faqs.a: Some people start to feel better after 1 or 2 weeks, but it can take 6 weeks for amitriptyline to work as a painkiller. The NHS advises allowing at least 6 weeks to see whether it works for pain. For depression, it usually takes between 4 and 6 weeks to feel the full benefit. It is best taken in the evening or before bed, because it can make a person sleepy.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking amitriptyline?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk with amitriptyline but may add to sleepiness. It is usually best to stop drinking until the effect of the medicine is known. The NHS also says it can be dangerous to take amitriptyline with methadone, stimulants such as MDMA or cocaine, and hallucinogens such as LSD. Cannabis can cause strong sleepiness and a fast heartbeat.

faqs.q: What should happen if too much amitriptyline has been taken?
faqs.a: Taking more than the prescribed dose can cause serious effects such as a change in heartbeat and seizures (fits). The NHS says to call 999 now if there is a fast or irregular heartbeat, a seizure, drowsiness or passing out, difficulty breathing, or sudden very bad confusion. It advises contacting NHS 111 for advice after taking more than the prescribed dose. The NHS says not to drive yourself to A&E.

faqs.q: Is it all right to stop amitriptyline suddenly?
faqs.a: Stopping suddenly can cause extra side effects, including flu-like symptoms. The NHS says to talk to a doctor before stopping. The doctor usually lowers the dose gradually over several weeks, or longer after long-term use. Stopping too soon in depression can bring the depression back, according to the NHS.

faqs.q: Can amitriptyline be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says amitriptyline can be taken during pregnancy and is not thought to be harmful to the baby. It says it can be taken while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy, because only very small amounts pass into breast milk. It has been linked with side effects in very few breastfed babies. The NHS says to tell the doctor about pregnancy, breastfeeding or plans to become pregnant before starting.
